EXERCITATIO TERTIA
De Fide, Scientia, & Opinione.

ART. I.
De firmitate, certitudine, & evidentia assensuum mentis nostrae.

1. Cum omnis habitus intellectivus, pro fine proximo habeat notitiam, sive assensum, quo mens assentitur iis propositionibus, quarum veritatem percipit & cognoscit; operae pretium erit, nonnihil praefari de assensu mentis, deque eius affectionibus, & speciebus, ideo ut intelligatur diversitas actuum mentis nostrae.

2. Assensus mentis, est judicium quo intellectus judicat propositionem aliquam esse veram: mens enim assentitur huic propositioni, homo est animal, eam amplectendo & approbando, hoc est, judicando eam esse veram.

3. Tres sunt gradus perfectionis, quos in assensu mentis observarunt Philosophi, videlicet firmitas, certitudo, & evidentia: quibus opponuntur totidem gradus imperfectionis, videlicet infirmitas seu vacillatio, incertitudo, & inevidentia.

4. Assensus firmus, est is qui est sine haesitatione, dubitatione, formidine partis oppositae. Infirmus vero, seu vacillans assensus, est cum mens ita assentitur huic vel illi propositioni, ut de eius veritate dubitet, aut saltem aliquo modo metuat ne isti propositioni assentendo erret.

5. Assensus certus, est qui nititur certo aliquo aut solido fundamento, non vero levi aut fallaci ratione. Assensus incertus, est qui contrario modo se habet. Hic diligenter notandum est, ad certitudinem assensus requiri, ut fundamentum quo mens nititur, dum assensum praebet, non solum sit in se certum, sed etiam assentienti tale videatur: nisi enim ille sciat rationem, qua nititur, esse certam, eius assensus nullo modo erit certus & stabilis.

6. Denique assensus evidens, est cum quis per se hoc est, vi sui sensus aut rationis, absque alterius informatione & testificatione percipit eam propositionem cui assentitur, esse veram: exempli gratia, cum video Socratem apud me stantem, assentior huic propositioni, Socrates stat: & assensus meus est evidens, idque quia non per alterius informationem aut testimonium, sed vi mei sensus, rem ita se habere percipio: item cum assentior huic propositioni, homo est animal, assensus est evidens, idque quia vi proprii intellectus, seu rationis, percipio homini inesse naturam sensitivam: adeoque quamvis nemo illud assereret, imo quamvis omnes contrarium assererent, istam propositionem veram esse judicarem.

7. Contra vero, inevidens est assensus, cum quis assentitur propositioni, non quod sensus aut solida ratio eam veram esse demonstret: sed vel quod levis aliqua ratio illud suadeat (levis enim ratio non pellit mentis tenebras, atque adeo facit assensum obscurum & inevidentem) vel quod alius testetur eam esse veram: sic qui vidit Petrum interfectum, & assensum praebet huic propositioni, Petrus est interfectus, eius assensus est evidens: qui vero propter hujus narrationem & testimonium, assensum praebet isti propositioni, eius assensus est inevidens, idque quia neque sensu, neque ratione percipit eam esse veram.

8. Hi tres gradus perfectionis, qui in assensu cernuntur, ita se habent, ut secundus includat primum, eique aliquid superaddat; tertius vero includat et primum et secundum, illisque aliquid superaddat: nam ut assensus sit firmus, satis est quod fundamentum, quo nititur ille assensus, assentienti certum et solidum videatur: quamvis enim revera non sit tale, si tamen assentienti tale esse videatur, is proculdubio firmiter et absque haesitatione assentietur: sic haeretici firmiter assentiuntur suis erroribus; quamvis enim fundamenta quibus nituntur, non sint certa & solida, iis tamen (quae eorum est caecitas) efficacissima et validissima videntur.

9. At vero ut assensus sit certus, et plane ab errore alienus, non tantum requiritur, ut fundamentum quo nititur, videatur assentienti certum, & solidum, sed etiam ut revera & in se tale sit; alioqui assensus noster erit erroneus, & falsus: quare quamvis haereticis attribui patiamur firmitatem in judicando, non tamen putamus iis competere certitudinem judicandi: certitudo enim & error simul consistere nequeunt.

10. Tandem vero, ut assensus sit evidens, non tantum requiritur, ut ejus fundamentum assentienti videatur certum et solidum, & etiam in se sit tale; sed etiam requiritur, ut illud fundamentum non sit alterius testimonium, vel narratio; sed vel sit sensus, vel solida aliqua ratio perspicue demonstrans rem ita se habere.

11. Quemadmodum igitur assensus potest esse firmus, quamvis non sit certus, ut videre est in Haereticis, absque ullo timore aut formidine assensum praebentibus iis dogmatis, quae Catholicae Fidei aut bonis moribus repugnant, ita etiam assensus potest esse certus, quamvis non sit evidens: qui enim assentitur propositioni alicui propter DEI testimonium in Sacra Scriptura propositum, ejus assensus proculdubio est valde certus, quia nititur certissimo fundamento, videlicet DEI testimonio, non tamen est evidens, non enim ideo assentitur Theologus, quod aut sensu aut ratione percipiat rem ita se habere, sed quod DEUS asserat, aut dicat rem ita se habere.

12. Ex his patet, hos tres gradus perfectionis, qui in assensu mentis cernuntur, ita se habere, ut primus latius pateat secundo, & secundus tertio; quemadmodum etiam in gradibus necessitatis kata meros latius patet quam kath hauto, & kath hauto quam kath hauto proton.
english: Third Exercise. On Faith, Science, and Opinion.
Article I. On the firmness, certainty, and evidence of the mind's acts of assent.

1. Every intellective habit has knowledge — or assent — as its proximate end: the mind assents to those propositions whose truth it perceives and cognizes. It is therefore worthwhile to premise something about the mind's assent, its affections, and its species, so that the diversity of our mind's acts may be understood.
2. Assent of the mind is the judgment by which the intellect judges some proposition true. The mind assents to "man is an animal" by embracing and approving it — that is, by judging it true.

3. Philosophers have marked three degrees of perfection in assent: firmness, certainty, and evidence. Opposed to them are three degrees of imperfection: infirmity or vacillation, uncertainty, and inevidence.

4. Firm assent is without hesitation, doubt, or fear of the opposite side. Infirm or vacillating assent is when the mind so assents that it doubts the proposition's truth, or at least somehow fears that by assenting it may err.

5. Certain assent rests on some certain or solid foundation, not on a light or fallacious reason. Uncertain assent is the contrary. Note carefully: for certainty it is required that the foundation on which the mind rests while assenting not only be certain in itself, but also appear such to the one who assents. Unless he knows that the reason on which he rests is certain, his assent will in no way be certain and stable.

6. Evident assent is when someone, by the force of his own sense or reason and apart from another's information or testimony, perceives that the proposition to which he assents is true. When I see Socrates standing near me and assent to "Socrates stands," my assent is evident — not by another's report, but by my own sense. Likewise when I assent to "man is an animal," the assent is evident because by my own intellect I perceive that a sensitive nature is in man. Even if no one asserted it — even if all asserted the contrary — I would still judge that proposition true.

7. Assent is inevident when someone assents not because sense or solid reason demonstrates the proposition true, but either because a light reason persuades it (a light reason does not drive away the mind's darkness, and so leaves the assent obscure and inevident) or because another testifies that it is true. He who has seen Peter slain and assents to "Peter is slain" has evident assent; he who assents only because of that man's narration has inevident assent, because neither sense nor reason shows him that it is true.

8. These three degrees so stand that the second includes the first and adds something; the third includes both and adds something further. For firmness it is enough that the foundation appear certain and solid to the one assenting. Even if in reality it is not such, if it appears such he will assent firmly and without hesitation. So heretics firmly assent to their errors: though their foundations are neither certain nor solid, to them — such is their blindness — they seem most efficacious and valid.

9. For certainty, and freedom from error, more is required: the foundation must not only appear certain and solid to the one assenting, but really and in itself be such. Otherwise the assent is erroneous and false. We may grant heretics firmness in judging; we do not grant them certainty of judging. Certainty and error cannot stand together.

10. For evidence still more is required: the foundation must appear certain and solid, and be such in itself — and it must not be another's testimony or narration, but either sense or some solid reason that clearly demonstrates that the matter so holds.

11. Assent can therefore be firm without being certain — as in heretics who without fear assent to dogmas that conflict with the Catholic faith or with good morals. Assent can also be certain without being evident. He who assents to a proposition because of God's testimony in Sacred Scripture has assent that is without doubt very certain, resting on the most certain foundation — God's own testimony — yet it is not evident. The theologian does not assent because sense or reason shows him that the matter so holds, but because God asserts or says that it so holds.

12. These three degrees of perfection in the mind's assent therefore stand so that the first extends more widely than the second, and the second than the third — just as among the degrees of necessity the "in a respect" sense extends more widely than the "in itself" sense, and that more widely than the "in itself primarily."

ART. II.
Quomodo inter se differant, scire, credere & opinari.

1. Omnis assensus mentis vel est actus sciendi, vel actus credendi, vel actus opinandi; quandocunque enim judicamus aliquid esse verum, vel certe scimus illud esse verum, vel credimus illud esse verum propter alterius testimonium; vel propter levem et inefficacem rationem opinamur illud esse verum.

2. Actus sciendi, cum opponitur actibus credendi & opinandi, late accipitur, pro quavis notitia actuali certa & evidente; quomodo accepta scientia non solum cernitur in disciplinis speculativis, sed etiam in practicis; nam in Philosophia morali, quae est disciplina practica, non opinamur, aut credimus, sed evidenter scimus actiones liberalitatis esse honestas, actiones vero vitiorum ei oppositorum esse inhonestas; in aedificatoria arte non opinantur aut credunt, sed evidenter sciunt periti Architecti bases in aedificiis esse ad libellam collocandas, columnas esse ad perpendiculum erigendas, aliaque similia: nec solum circa universalia, sed etiam singularia versatur haec notitia. Nam cum video Petrum stantem, aut audio Petrum loquentem, non opinor, aut credo, sed scio Petrum loqui & stare.

3. Hujus divisionis sufficientia sic demonstratur: omnis assensus mentis vel nititur testimonio, vel ratione: si nititur testimonio, est fides actualis, seu actus credendi; si vero nititur ratione, vel nititur ratione certa & solida, estque scientia; vel nititur ratione tantum probabili, estque opinio.

4. Assensus nitens alterius testimonio, vel nititur testimonio divino, & a Scholasticis appellatur fides divina; vel nititur testimonio humano, & appellatur fides humana.

5. Hic obiter notare possumus Pontificiorum errorem; qui nobiscum fatentur, eam fidem non divinam sed humanam esse, quae praecipue testimonio hominum nititur; & nihilominus audacissime asseverant, assensum, quem praebemus articulis fidei & ipsi sacrae Scripturae, unde illi articuli colliguntur, niti testimonio Ecclesiae (ut vocant) representativae, h. e. Episcoporum & Pastorum in generali concilio congregatorum; item Ecclesiae (ut ipsi loquuntur) virtualis, h. e. ipsius Pontificis Romani: atque ita aut fateri cogentur, omnem fidem viatorum humanam esse, penitus videlicet sublata fide divina, aut eorum Episcopos non homines sed DEOS indigitandos esse.

6. Pulchra institui potest comparatio inter scientiam, opinionem, & fidem divinam: scientia enim est assensus firmus, certus, & evidens; fides divina est assensus firmus & certus, sed non evidens; opinio denique etsi aliquando sit assensus firmus, h. e. sine haesitatione aut dubitatione, saepe tamen neque est firmus, neque certus, neque evidens.

7. Scientia est assensus firmus; quia is qui scit propositionem aliquam esse veram, non dubitanter aut haesitanter assentitur, sed firmiter: est assensus certus, quia is qui scit, nititur solido aliquo fundamento; alioqui non sciret, sed opinaretur: denique est evidens, quia sciens non ideo assentitur, quod alius testetur eam propositionem esse veram, sed quod ipse vi alicujus evidentis argumenti, percipiat rem ita se habere.

8. Fides divina est assensus firmus, quia illi qui in DEUM credunt, non haesitant, aut dubitant de veritate historiae sacrae, & promissionum divinarum: est assensus certus, quia nititur certissimo fundamento, videlicet DEI testimonio, qui est ipsa veritas: non tamen est evidens; is enim qui credit, non ideo assentitur, quod sensu aut ratione percipiat rem ita se habere, sed quod DEUS hoc testetur & asserat.

9. Hinc patet, quam egregie Apostolus, undecimo ad Hebraeos, versu primo, naturam fidei divinae expresserit; cum enim dicit eam esse hypostasin, indicat ejus firmitatem & certitudinem; cum vero dicit eam esse elenchon pragmaton ou blepomenon, ejus inevidentiam & obscuritatem enigmaticam declarat.

10. Opinio aliquando potest esse assensus firmus, (nonnunquam enim homines ita moventur levibus rationibus, ut eas pro validissimis argumentis habeant, ideoque absque ulla haesitatione aut formidine partis oppositae assentiuntur;) nunquam vero est certus aut evidens: is enim qui opinatur, vel nititur levibus rationibus, vel hominum testimoniis, quae nunquam pariunt nobis aut certitudinem aut evidentiam judicandi.

11. Dicet aliquis, hanc comparationem fidei, scientiae, & opinionis, quam jam attulimus, derogare de dignitate fidei; ex ea enim sequitur, quamlibet scientiam esse perfectiorem assensum fide, quia viz. deest fidei evidentia, quae tamen competit scientiae. Respond. Scientiam esse perfectiorem fide secundum quid, quia viz. est assensus evidens; fidem vero esse perfectiorem qualibet scientia simpliciter & absolute; idque propter duas rationes. 1. enim fides versatur circa nobilissimum objectum, h. e. circa magnum illud mysterium pietatis, DEUM in carne revelatum, justificatum in spiritu, conspectum ab Angelis, & praedicatum Gentibus. 2. Fides nititur certissimo fundamento, h. e. DEI ipsius testimonio, qui ipsa veritas est, quique nec fallere nec falli potest.
english: Article II. How knowing, believing, and opining differ from one another.

1. Every assent of the mind is an act of knowing, of believing, or of opining. Whenever we judge something true, either we certainly know it, or we believe it because of another's testimony, or we opine it because of a light and inefficacious reason.

2. The act of knowing, opposed to believing and opining, is taken broadly for any actual certain and evident knowledge. Science so taken appears not only in speculative disciplines but in practical ones. In moral philosophy we do not opine or believe but evidently know that acts of liberality are honorable and the opposed vices dishonorable. Skilled architects do not opine or believe but evidently know that foundations must be set to the level and columns to the perpendicular. This knowledge concerns singulars as well as universals: when I see Peter standing or hear him speaking, I do not opine or believe — I know that he speaks and stands.

3. The division is sufficient: every assent rests either on testimony or on reason. If on testimony, it is actual faith — an act of believing. If on reason, either on certain and solid reason (science) or on merely probable reason (opinion).
4. Assent on another's testimony is either divine faith (on divine testimony) or human faith (on human testimony), as the Scholastics speak.

5. Note the Papists' error in passing. They grant with us that faith resting chiefly on men's testimony is human, not divine; yet they boldly claim that our assent to the articles of faith and to Scripture itself rests on the testimony of the "representative" Church — bishops and pastors in general council — and of the "virtual" Church, the Roman Pontiff. They must either confess that all wayfarers' faith is human (divine faith abolished) or call their bishops not men but gods.

6. Compare science, opinion, and divine faith. Science is firm, certain, and evident assent. Divine faith is firm and certain, but not evident. Opinion is sometimes firm (without hesitation), yet often neither firm nor certain nor evident.

7. Science is firm because the knower assents without doubt or hesitation; certain because he rests on a solid foundation — else he would opine, not know; evident because he assents not because another testifies, but because by some evident argument he himself perceives that the matter so holds.

8. Divine faith is firm because believers in God do not hesitate about sacred history and the divine promises; certain because it rests on God's testimony, who is truth itself; yet not evident — for the believer assents not because sense or reason shows him that the matter so holds, but because God testifies and asserts it.

9. So the Apostle in Hebrews 11:1 excellently expressed divine faith's nature: calling it hypostasis he marks its firmness and certainty; calling it the evidence of things not seen he declares its inevidence and enigmatic obscurity.

10. Opinion can sometimes be firm — people take light reasons for strongest arguments and assent without fear of the opposite — but it is never certain or evident. The one who opines rests on light reasons or men's testimonies, which never yield certainty or evidence of judging.

11. Does this comparison derogate from faith's dignity, since any science would then be a more perfect assent than faith for want of evidence? Answer: science is more perfect than faith in a respect, because it is evident assent; but faith is more perfect than any science simply and absolutely — for two reasons. First, faith concerns the noblest object: that great mystery of godliness — God revealed in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached to the nations. Second, faith rests on the most certain foundation: God's own testimony, who is truth itself and can neither deceive nor be deceived.

ART. III.
An fides semper sit elenchos pragmaton ou blepomenon.

1. Ostensum est superiori articulo, fidem omnem, sive sit divina, sive humana, esse assensum inevidentem; & ob id Apostolum 11. ad Hebraeos, vers.1. asserere fidem esse elenchon pragmaton ou blepomenon; idem etiam confirmari potest ex 1 Corinth. cap.13. vers.12. ubi Apostolus asserit, nos nunc videre per speculum, & in enigmate. Item ex doctrina ejusdem Apostoli, de cessatione & evacuatione fidei, quae futura est in patria; ideo enim fides evacuari dicitur, & non perfici, sicut charitas, quia imperfectionem, nimirum obscuritatem & inevidentiam, in sui ratione & essentia involvit: quare Augustinus in illud Johannis 14. vado parare vobis locum, egregie dicit, eat DOMINUS, ut paret locum; eat, ut videatur, lateat, ut credatur. Similiter docet Gregorius, Hom. 16. in Evang. & lib. Dial. cap.5. apparentia (inquit) non habent fidem, sed agnitionem: & iterum: hoc veraciter dicitur credi, quod non valet videri.

2. Ut autem hoc planius evadat, afferami & solvam ea argumenta, quae probant ea etiam quae videntur vel sciuntur, sub fidei objecto comprehendi: quale imprimis est illud DOMINI ad discipulos, Johanne 14. dixi vobis priusquam fiat, ut cum factum fuerit, credatis: hinc enim colligitur, fidem esse aliquando rerum per experientiam cognitarum, atque adeo visarum.

3. Deinde Johan.20. cum dixisset Thomas Apostolus, nisi videro, non credam; CHRISTUM videlicet redivivum; dixit ei DOMINUS jam credenti, quia vidisti me Thoma, credidisti.

4. Tertio; caeteri quoque Apostoli & Virgo Maria, multique alii fideles, quod viderunt hoc crediderunt; CHRISTUM videlicet hominem, passum, mortuum, sepultum, a mortuis resurgentem, & in coelos ascendentem, et alia multa quae ipsis fidei articulis expressa sunt: unde Joh. Epist.1. ait, quod audivimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod perspeximus, & manus nostrae contrectaverunt, de verbo vitae annuntiamus vobis.

5. Quarto: Philosophus aliquis sciens per Demonstrationem, unum DEUM esse omnium rerum principium & causam, potest ejusdem propositionis accipere fidem, manente priori cognitione; si videlicet e Pagano fiat Christianus: is ergo simul habebit fidem & scientiam, ejusque fides pro objecto habebit res evidenter scitas seu visas.

6. Ut haec argumenta tollantur, primo ponam aliquot fundamenta, ex quibus horum argumentorum solutiones colligi possunt; deinde Fonsecae, Estii, & aliorum pravam doctrinam de repugnantia fidei & scientiae confutabo. Primum fundamentum sit hoc: Fides seu to credere saepenumero in Scriptura, & apud probatos Authores generaliter accipitur, pro eo quod est quovis modo assentiri & judicare aliquid verum esse: sic enim dicitur aliquis oculis suis credere, & apud Dialecticos qualecunque argumentum fidem facere dicitur.

7. Secundum fundamentum est: S. Thomam, aliosque Apostolos & fideles, aliud vidisse, aliud credidisse: hominem enim viderunt, & DEUM crediderunt: h.e. ut ait Augustinus; Cernebant hominem viventem quem viderant morientem, & credebant DEUM in carne latentem; & alibi, apparuit inter homines homo, offerens HOMINEM videntibus, DEUM servans credentibus.

8. Tertium fundamentum: fides dicitur assensus inevidens; item dicitur esse elenchos pragmaton ou blepomenon, non quod ea quae creduntur omnino inevidentia sint, & nullo modo videantur; sed quod quatenus creduntur, inevidentia sint, seu quod non habeant evidentiam ab eo propter quod creduntur. In hoc enim differt fides a scientia, quod fundamentum quo nititur scientia (h.e. medium demonstrationis) per evidentiam rei intellectum convincat, causas ejus aperiendo; fundamentum vero quo nititur fides (videlicet DEI authoritas) intellectum convincat, non per evidentiam rei cui assentimur, sed per certitudinem suam & infallibilitatem. Cum igitur munus fidei, non sit efficere ut res obscurae fiant perspicuae, sed efficere ut intellectus cedat authoritati dicentis, & sic assentiatur; manifestum est ea quae creduntur quatenus creduntur esse inevidentia, seu non habere evidentiam a fundamento suo propter quod creduntur: vide D. Pareum de justificatione, lib. 2. cap.5. & D. Richardum Field, de Eccl. lib.4. cap.8. Caeterum hoc non impedit, quo minus ea quae creduntur alia ratione evidentia sint, & ex se manifesta vel sensibus externis vel rationi: sicut enim una & eadem propositio, quatenus est conclusio demonstrationis judicatur esse necessaria, & non posse aliter se habere; quatenus vero est conclusio probabilis syllogismi, judicatur ab eodem homine contingens, & posse aliter se habere: ita etiam articuli quidam fidei, quatenus ab Apostolis sensu percipiebantur, aut a nobis ratione manifesta demonstrantur, evidentiam habent & claritatem; quatenus vero creduntur propter DEI testantis authoritatem, evidentiam illam non habent, & ob id recte dicuntur pragmata ou blepomena.
english: Article III. Whether faith is always the evidence of things not seen.

1. The previous article showed that every faith — divine or human — is inevident assent. Hence the Apostle in Hebrews 11:1 calls faith the evidence of things not seen. The same is confirmed by 1 Corinthians 13:12 (we now see through a glass, in an enigma) and by the Apostle's teaching that faith will cease and be evacuated in the homeland — not perfected, as charity is — because obscurity and inevidence belong to faith's very notion and essence. So Augustine on John 14 ("I go to prepare a place for you"): let the Lord go that he may prepare a place; go that he may be seen, be hidden that he may be believed. Gregory likewise: appearances have not faith but recognition; what cannot be seen is truly said to be believed.

2. To make this plainer I will solve arguments that put even seen or known things under faith's object. First, the Lord's word in John 14: I have told you before it comes to pass, that when it is come to pass you may believe — as if faith were sometimes of things known by experience and so seen.
3. Next John 20: Thomas said, unless I see I will not believe (Christ risen); the Lord said to him already believing, because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed.

4. Third: the other Apostles, the Virgin Mary, and many faithful believed what they saw — Christ as man, suffered, dead, buried, risen, ascended, and much else in the articles of faith. So 1 John: what we have heard, seen with our eyes, looked upon, and handled of the word of life, we announce to you.

5. Fourth: a philosopher who knows by demonstration that one God is principle and cause of all can, becoming a Christian from a pagan, receive faith of the same proposition while the prior cognition remains — and so have faith and science together, faith having for object things evidently known or seen.

6. To remove these arguments I first set foundations, then confute Fonseca, Estius, and others on the supposed repugnance of faith and science. First: "faith" or "to believe" is often taken in Scripture and among approved authors for assenting in any way that something is true — as when one "believes his eyes," or dialecticians say an argument "makes faith."

7. Second: St Thomas and the other Apostles and faithful saw one thing and believed another — a man seen, God believed. Augustine: they beheld a living man whom they had seen dying, and believed God hidden in the flesh; a man appeared among men, offering man to those who see, keeping God for those who believe.

8. Third: faith is called inevident assent and the evidence of things not seen — not because the things believed are altogether unseen, but because insofar as they are believed they lack evidence from that on account of which they are believed. Science's foundation (the middle of demonstration) convinces by the thing's evidence, opening causes; faith's foundation (God's authority) convinces by its certainty and infallibility, not by the evidence of the thing assented to. Faith's office is not to make obscure things clear, but to make the intellect yield to the speaker's authority. So things believed, as believed, are inevident (see Pareus; Field). Yet they may be evident in another respect — to sense or reason. One proposition can be necessary as a demonstration's conclusion and contingent as a probable syllogism's; so certain articles of faith have clarity insofar as the Apostles perceived them by sense or we demonstrate them by reason, but insofar as they are believed because of God's testifying authority they lack that evidence and are rightly called things not seen.

ART. IV.
An fides possit esse simul cum scientia de eadem propositione, & in eodem intellectu.

1. Quaeritur solet de scientia & fide, utrum unus & idem homo possit simul credere & scire eam propositionem cui assentitur esse veram, an vero tanta sit repugnantia fidei & scientiae, ut simul in eodem intellectu existere nequeant. In hac controversia, tanta est opinionum varietas, ut vix invenias duos celebres viros de ea idem sentientes: primo enim Scotus, in 3. Sent. Dist. 24. quaestione unica dicit, Neque actus, neque habitus fidei & scientiae posse simul in eodem intellectu existere circa idem subjectum.

2. Secundo, Durandus, quaest. 1. prologi Sent. & lib. 3. Sent. dist. 24. quaest.4. plane contrarium statuit, dicens fidem & scientiam circa eandem propositionem & in eodem intellectu simul existere posse, tam secundum actum, quam secundum habitum. Tertio, Petrus Fonseca, in lib.6. Metaph. cont. qu.1. Sect. 5. asserit habitus fidei & scientiae posse existere in eodem intellectu, & de eodem subjecto, ita tamen ut actus ab iis productus non sit actus fidei, sed scientia quaedam, eaque supernaturalis, propter concursum fidei ad eum producendum. Quarto: Guilielmus Estius, Duacensis Theologus, in 3. Sent. dist. 24. Art. 3. tria asserit: 1. habitus fidei & scientiae posse simul existere in eodem intellectu, & de eodem objecto. 2. Utrumque habitum diversis temporibus posse suum actum exercere. 3. Actum quem tunc elicit habitus fidei, non esse fidem consideratam secundum totam amplitudinem suae significationis: hoc est, secundum omnes conditiones in ea requisitas, quia videlicet non est inevidens rei notitia.

3. Quinta sententia, eaque verissima, est acutissimi Doctoris Antonii Ruvii Rhodensis, in suo opusculo de habitibus, tractatu 3. quaest. 3. ubi etiam tria innuit: primo, hos habitus posse simul esse in eodem intellectu, & de eodem objecto. 2. Utrumque habitum diversis temporibus posse suum actum exercere, sed non eodem tempore. 3. Actus ab illis habitibus, diversis temporibus elicitos, esse veros & proprie dictos illorum habituum actus, & per praesentiam habitus sciendi nihil derogari de proprietate actus credendi. Dico Ruvium haec tantum innuere, quia expresse & directe ibi loquitur solummodo de scientia & opinione; eadem autem ratio est scientiae et fidei, quoad possibilitatem & impossibilitatem coexistendi, ut cuivis manifestum est.

4. Primo igitur probatur contra Scotum; habitus fidei & scientiae posse simul esse in eodem subjecto, et circa idem objectum, idque hac ratione: Si quid impedit quo minus hi habitus in eodem intellectu coexistant, illud maxime est repugnantia actuum ad quos referuntur: Sed hoc non impedit: Ergo &c. Probatur assumptio; Habitus nihil sunt aliud, nisi faciles & expeditae potentiae ad actus: sed non est absurdum, aliqua habere simul potentias ad repugnantes actus, quos potest diversis temporibus exercere, licet simul non possit exercere utrumque: nam simul habemus potentiam ad flendum, et potentiam ad ridendum: item potentiam ambulandi, et potentiam sedendi; quamvis harum potentiarum actus adeo repugnantes sint, ut non possint uni subjecto simul inesse. Secundo, potest aliquis, qui per fidem novit mundum a DEO fuisse creatum, postea per Demonstrationem acquirere scientiam de Creatione Mundi, qua producta & acquisita non destruitur fides de illo articulo; sic enim non liceret homini Christiano, Metaphysicae & Physicae operam dare, ex quibus colliguntur Demonstrationes de creatione Mundi: non enim licet ea facere quae fidem aut destruunt, aut imminuunt.

5. Secundo: probatur contra Durandum, non esse possibile, ut intellectus eodem tempore, hoc est, uno et eodem instanti eliciat, et inevidentem assensum fidei, et evidentem assensum scientiae, quia sicut impossibile est, ut homo per sensum visus eandem rem eodem tempore distincte & confuse videat, ita etiam impossibile est, ut homo per intellectum, qui est animi oculus, eandem rem eodem instanti evidenter et inevidenter percipiat; ideoque impossibile est, ut simul habeat duos actus; unum evidentem, scientiae, alterum inevidentem, fidei.

6. Tertio: probatur contra Fonsecam et Estium; habitum fidei, quamvis in eodem intellectu coexistentem habeat habitum scientiae, posse elicere verum et proprie dictum actum fidei, idque secundum omnes conditiones in actu credendi requisitas: et proinde fidem et scientiam posse esse in eodem intellectu, & de eadem propositione, hoc etiam quoad actus; sed diversis temporibus elicitos: ratio est haec: potest aliquis fidelis, etiam post acquisitam scientiam de creatione mundi, ita apud se statuere: Ego tam firmiter assentior huic propositioni, DEUS creavit mundum; propter DEI testantis authoritatem, ut quamvis per rationem aliquam non perciperem mundum esse a DEO creatum; imo quamvis corrupta ratio contrarium dictitaret, assentirer tamen isti propositioni sine ulla formidine aut metu.

7. Hoc judicium mentis sine controversia provenit a sola fide, non scientia & fide simul, estque verus & proprie dictus fidei actus; hoc est, non deest ei ulla conditio in actu credendi requisita: prius probatur contra Fonsecam; quia neque scientia, neque aliquis alius naturalis habitus potest aliquid tale dictitare. Posterius etiam probatur, tum contra Fonsecam, tum contra Estium; quia assensus iste nititur sola authoritate testantis: est inevidens: consequentiae ratio est, quod assensus iste sit inevidens, cujus fundamentum quo nititur non valet parere evidentiam, sed certitudinem tantum; at hic assensus est talis; nam authoritas testantis non convincit intellectum nostrum per evidentiam & claritatem rei, sed per suam certitudinem & irrefragabilitatem. Ratio probabilis majoris est haec: talis est assensus, quale est medium & fundamentum quo nititur: Si enim medium sit certum, possitque intellectum nostrum certificare, & ut tale cognoscatur ab assentiente, noster assensus est certus: Si vero non ita se habet, est incertus: Ergo pari ratione, si medium valeat parere evidentiam intelligendi, assensus est evidens: si vero non valeat, est inevidens.
english: Article IV. Whether faith can coexist with science of the same proposition in the same intellect.

1. The question is whether one and the same person can at once believe and know the proposition to which he assents, or whether faith and science so repugn that they cannot coexist in one intellect. Opinions diverge so widely that two celebrated men scarcely agree. Scotus holds that neither act nor habit of faith and of science can coexist in the same intellect about the same subject.

2. Durandus holds the contrary: faith and science can coexist about the same proposition in the same intellect, as to both act and habit. Fonseca: the habits can coexist about the same subject, yet the act produced is not an act of faith but a certain supernatural science, because faith concurs in producing it. Estius: (1) the habits can coexist about the same object; (2) each can exercise its act at different times; (3) the act the habit of faith then elicits is not faith in the full amplitude of its meaning — not according to all required conditions — because it is not inevident knowledge of the thing.

3. The fifth and truest view is Antonio Rubio's: (1) these habits can be together in the same intellect about the same object; (2) each can exercise its act at different times, but not at the same time; (3) acts elicited at different times are true and proper acts of those habits, and the habit of knowing derogates nothing from the act of believing. Rubio speaks there of science and opinion, but the same reason holds for science and faith.

4. Against Scotus: the habits can coexist. What would impede them is chiefly repugnance of their acts — but that does not impede. Habits are easy potencies for acts; we can have at once potencies for repugnant acts exercised at different times (weeping and laughing, walking and sitting) though not both acts at once. Further: one who by faith knows God created the world can later acquire demonstrative science of creation without destroying that faith — else a Christian could not study metaphysics and physics, from which such demonstrations are gathered, and one may not do what destroys or diminishes faith.

5. Against Durandus: the intellect cannot in one and the same instant elicit both faith's inevident assent and science's evident assent. As sight cannot see the same thing at once distinctly and confusedly, so the intellect (the soul's eye) cannot perceive the same thing at once evidently and inevidently.

6. Against Fonseca and Estius: even while coexisting with the habit of science, the habit of faith can elicit a true and proper act of faith with all conditions required for believing — so faith and science can be in the same intellect about the same proposition as to acts, but elicited at different times. A believer, even after acquiring science of creation, can resolve: I so firmly assent that God created the world because of God's testifying authority that even if reason did not show it — even if corrupt reason said the contrary — I would still assent without fear.

7. That judgment comes from faith alone, not from science and faith together, and is a true act of faith. Neither science nor any natural habit can dictate such a resolve. The assent rests on the testifier's authority alone and is inevident: a foundation that yields certainty but not evidence makes the assent inevident; God's authority convinces by certainty and irrefragability, not by the thing's clarity. As the medium is, so is the assent — certain or uncertain, evident or inevident.

ART. V.
De fidei divisione in explicitam, & implicitam; & an inevidentia, quam fidei tribuimus, faciat pro caeca & implicita Pontificiorum fide.

1. Theologi dividunt fidem in explicitam et implicitam, vel ut loquitur Lombardus, lib. 3. Sent. Dist. 25. in distinctam, & velatam seu confusam: hujus distinctionis explicationem legere possumus apud clarissimum Tilenum, parte prima Syntagmatis, Disp. 38. Thes.23. & 24. item apud Durandum, lib. 3. Sent. dist. 25. quaest. 1. S. Thomam, 2.2. q. 2. Art. 7. Guilielmum Estium, lib. 3. Sent. Dist.25. ex quibus authoribus descriptiones istius divisionis bene colligi possunt: fides explicita, est qua aliquid creditur secundum se distincte, & in particulari. Implicita vero, est qua aliquid creditur non in se, sed in alio, tanquam in universali; Exempli gratia, Christiani rudes & simpliciores (ut loquuntur) qui ea sola intelligunt, quae ad salutem absolute necessaria sunt, ut articulos fidei, decalogum, & caetera, cum ex animo profitentur se credere S. Scripturam esse DEI verbum, & proinde fide dignam, habent suae fidei objectum; unum generale, quod formaliter, explicite, & per se credunt: alterum particulare, quod implicite & ex consequenti credunt: objectum generale, quod explicite credunt, est Scripturam esse DEI verbum; & proinde fidem ei adhibendam esse: objecta particularia, quae implicite in illo generali & ex consequenti credunt, sunt historiae & dogmata Scripturae, quorum cognitionem nondum assecuti sunt, ut Noachum habuisse tres filios, Abrahamum duos, non ablatum esse sceptrum a Juda ante adventum Messiae: qui enim credunt Scripturam totam esse veram, illi implicite & ex consequenti credunt omnia esse vera quae in Scriptura continentur, hoc est, habent fidem implicitam omnium historiarum, dogmatum, & praedictionum Propheticarum, quae sunt in sacrae Scripturae volumine, omnium (inquam) quorum particularem & distinctam notitiam non acquisiverunt.

2. Quaeritur hic potest, an haec divisio fidei in explicitam & implicitam, in Scholis Ecclesiarum reformatarum ferenda sit; Respond. Duabus assertionibus: prior est haec; praedicta distinctio fidei admitti potest, si sano modo concipiatur: certum enim est non solum Laicos & simpliciores, sed etiam clarissimos & doctissimos Theologos quaedam implicite credere in isto generali quod Scriptura sit DEI verbum & proinde fide dignissima; quaedam (inquam) quorum distinctam intelligentiam nondum assecuti sunt: hoc enim patet ex quotidiano nostro in cognitione Scripturae progressu, qui tamen non arguit Scripturae ipsius obscuritatem (ut nugantur Pontificii) sed ingenii nostri imbecillitatem, & mysteriorum coelestium, quae in Scriptura passim traduntur, immensam opulentiam, quae sensim angusto illi vasi mentis humanae infunditur, non autem tota simul infundi potest.

3. Secunda assertio est haec; praedicta divisio fidei Christianae, si ita accipiatur ut a Pontificiis accipi solet, rejicienda est tanquam crassa, absurda, & naturae fidei prorsus contraria: illi enim per fidem implicitam intelligunt eam fidem qua laici ignota & nondum intellecta fidei dogmata credunt implicite in illo generali, quod vera sunt omnia quae Romana Ecclesia credit & pro veris amplectitur; quae quidem fides non est divina, sed humana; id est, non nititur DEI, sed hominum testimonio: non est hypostasis aut elenchos, sed levis & fallax conjectura, quae non DEI verbo, sed hominum judicio per se infirmo, atque adeo fragili admodum & ruinoso fundamento nititur.

4. Quaeritur etiam potest; an inevidentia quam non solum Theologi Sententiarii, sed etiam Orthodoxi Doctores fidei attribuunt, faciat pro caeca illa & implicita Pontificiorum fide: maximus enim & confusus ille assensus, qui solo Ecclesiae Romanae testimonio nititur (ut id quod res est dicam) maxime est inevidens. Respond. Inevidentiam nihil pro eorum sententia facere: quia inevidentia illa non excludit omnem notitiam, sed eam solam quae nititur medio scientifico; id est, sensu aut evidente ratione a natura rei petita. Secundo, quia certitudo, quae est secunda fidei conditio, necessario praesupponit firmam notitiam & persuasionem de doctrina, cui assentimur, quod non sit hominis sed DEI verbum: talis autem notitia aut persuasio implicitae Pontificiorum fidei velut e regione adversatur, ac proinde in ea certitudo inveniri non potest.
english: Article V. On the division of faith into explicit and implicit; and whether the inevidence we ascribe to faith favors the blind and implicit faith of the Papists.

1. Theologians divide faith into explicit and implicit — Lombard's distinct and veiled or confused (Tilenus, Durandus, Thomas, Estius). Explicit faith believes something distinctly in itself and in particular. Implicit faith believes something not in itself but in another, as in a universal. Simpler Christians who grasp only what is absolutely necessary to salvation — articles, Decalogue, and the like — when they sincerely hold Scripture to be God's word and worthy of faith, believe that general object explicitly, and believe particular histories and dogmas of Scripture (Noah's three sons, Abraham's two, the scepter not taken from Judah before the Messiah) implicitly and by consequence in that general. Those who believe the whole Scripture true have implicit faith of all its histories, dogmas, and prophecies whose distinct knowledge they have not yet acquired.

2. May Reformed schools admit this division? First assertion: yes, if soundly conceived. Not only laypeople but the most learned theologians believe some things implicitly under the general that Scripture is God's word — things they have not yet distinctly understood. Daily progress in knowing Scripture shows not Scripture's obscurity (as Papists claim) but our mind's weakness and the immense wealth of heavenly mysteries poured little by little into the narrow vessel of the human mind.

3. Second assertion: taken as the Papists take it, the division is crude, absurd, and contrary to faith's nature. Their "implicit faith" is laypeople believing unknown dogmas under the general that whatever the Roman Church believes is true. That is human faith, not divine — resting on men's testimony, not God's; a light conjecture on a fragile foundation, not hypostasis or elenchos.

4. Does the inevidence Orthodox doctors ascribe to faith favor that blind Papist faith? That confused assent on Rome's testimony alone is most inevident — yet inevidence does not help them. It excludes only scientific knowledge (sense or evident reason from the thing's nature), not all knowledge. Certainty, faith's second condition, presupposes firm persuasion that what we assent to is God's word, not man's. That persuasion is opposed to Papist implicit faith; certainty cannot be found in it.

ART. VI.
De triplici lumine, videlicet naturae, fidei seu gratiae, & gloriae.

1. In Theologia Scholastica variae inveniuntur distinctiones petitae ab istis tribus terminis: natura, gratia, & gloria. Prima est, qua DEI Opt. Max. regnum distinguitur, in regnum naturae, regnum gratiae, & regnum gloriae. Regnum naturae, est naturale illud imperium, quod DEUS habet in omnes res creatas, quas pro arbitrio regit & gubernat. Regnum gratiae, est quo DEUS regnat in Ecclesia sua in terris militante. Regnum gloriae est, quo regnat in Ecclesia in coelis triumphante.

2. Secunda distinctio est qua DEI localis praesentia distinguitur in praesentiam naturalem, seu essentialem, gratiosam, & gloriosam. Secundum praesentiam naturalem DEUS est ubique: per praesentiam gratiosam DEUS dicitur esse in justis & sanctis hominibus, & vicissim illi habitaculum & Templum DEI dicuntur; & per praesentiam gloriosam Deus dicitur esse in coelis, ubi gloriam suam & majestatem beatis hominibus & Angelis manifestat.

3. Tertia divisio est qua opera DEI ad extra dividuntur in opera naturae, opera gratiae, & opera gloriae. Opera naturae, sunt rerum visibilium & invisibilium creatio, conservatio, & cum iisdem cooperatio in omnibus earum actionibus: nam in eo vivimus, movemur, & sumus. Opera gratiae, sunt Verbi incarnatio, humiliatio, exaltatio, triplex ejus officium, videlicet Regium, Propheticum, & Sacerdotale: item electorum per verbi praedicationem & Sacramentorum administrationem efficax vocatio, eorundemque regeneratio, justificatio, sanctificatio, & conservatio in statu gratiae. Opera gloriae, sunt electorum glorificatio, & reproborum aeterna damnatio.

4. Quarta distinctio, est qua vita humana dividitur in vitam naturae, vitam gratiae, & vitam gloriae. Vita naturae est, qua vivimus vitam animalem & rationalem. Vita gratiae, est vita spiritualis, qua vivimus DEO per fidem & charitatem. Vita gloriae, est vita beata, qua in patria DEUM facie ad faciem videbimus.

5. Quinta divisio, est qua consilium & decretum DEI distinguitur in decretum naturae, gratiae, & gloriae — seu quo DEUS ordinat res naturales, res gratiae, & res gloriae.

6. Sexta & ad propositum maxime spectans distinctio, est qua lumen seu cognitio mentis humanae distinguitur in lumen naturae, lumen fidei seu gratiae, & lumen gloriae. Lumen naturae, est naturalis illa vis intelligendi, qua homo, etiam lapsus, percipit principia per se nota, & ex iis conclusionibus ratiocinando assequitur notitiam rerum naturalium. Lumen fidei seu gratiae, est supernaturalis illuminatio, qua credimus ea quae DEUS in Scriptura revelavit, & quae supra captum rationis naturalis elevantur. Lumen gloriae, est illa perfecta cognitio DEI, qua beati in patria DEUM nude & intuitive vident.

7. Ex his patet, lumen fidei medium esse inter lumen naturae & lumen gloriae: perfectius est lumine naturae, quia versatur circa objecta sublimiora, & nititur certiore fundamento; imperfectius est lumine gloriae, quia non est intuitiva DEI visio, sed assensus inevidens nitens DEI testimonio.

8. Pontificii non contenti isto triplici lumine, fingunt lumen aliquod propheticum, seu speciale donum, quo Doctores Ecclesiae, & praesertim Pontifex Romanus, infallibiliter de rebus fidei judicent. Sed hoc commentum nullo Scripturae testimonio nititur, & fidem viatorum transfert a DEI verbo ad hominum judicia.
english: Article VI. On the threefold light: of nature, of faith or grace, and of glory.

1. Scholastic theology draws several distinctions from nature, grace, and glory. First: God's kingdom — of nature (his empire over all creatures), of grace (reign in the Church militant), and of glory (reign in the Church triumphant).
2. Second: God's presence — natural or essential (everywhere), gracious (in the just, who are his temple), and glorious (in heaven, manifesting majesty to the blessed).

3. Third: works ad extra — of nature (creation, conservation, cooperation — in him we live and move and are); of grace (the Word's incarnation, humiliation, exaltation, threefold office; effectual calling, regeneration, justification, sanctification); of glory (the elect's glorification and the reprobate's damnation).
4. Fourth: human life — natural (animal and rational), of grace (spiritual life to God by faith and charity), and of glory (seeing God face to face in the homeland).
5. Fifth: God's decree as ordering things of nature, grace, and glory.

6. Sixth, and most to our purpose: the mind's light — of nature (fallen man's power to grasp self-evident principles and natural conclusions); of faith or grace (supernatural illumination believing what Scripture reveals above natural reason); of glory (the blessed's naked, intuitive vision of God).
7. Faith's light stands between nature and glory: above nature (loftier objects, surer foundation), below glory (not intuition but inevident assent on God's testimony).

8. Papists invent a further "prophetic" light by which Church doctors — especially the Roman Pontiff — judge faith infallibly. Scripture does not support it; it shifts wayfarers' faith from God's word to men's judgments.

ART. VII.
An detur in viatoribus lumen aliquod clarius fidei lumine.

1. Theologia dividi solet in Theologiam viatorum & Theologiam comprehensorum, seu in Theologiam viae & Theologiam patriae. Theologia viatorum nititur lumine fidei; Theologia patriae lumine gloriae. Quaeritur an praeter lumen fidei detur viatoribus aliquod lumen clarius, quo mysteria fidei evidenter cognoscant.

2. Pontificii & nonnulli Scholastici affirmant dari lumen aliquod propheticum, seu donum intellectus & sapientiae, quo Doctores Ecclesiae clarius & evidentius de mysteriis fidei judicent quam vulgares fideles. Sed Orthodoxi negant dari viatoribus lumen ullo modo clarius lumine fidei quoad evidentiam rei; quamvis admittere possimus gradus in ipso lumine fidei quoad extensionem & firmitatem.

3. Ratio est: fides in sui ratione involvit inevidentiam; si daretur lumen clarius quo res fidei evidenter perciperentur, desinerent esse objecta fidei & fierent objecta scientiae seu visionis. At in via non datur visio DEI, sed fides: 2 Cor.5.7. per fidem ambulamus, non per speciem.

4. Quod vero doctiores Theologi plura credibilia intelligunt & melius explicant, id non provenit ex lumine clariore quam sit lumen fidei, sed ex majore eruditione, majore assiduitate in Scripturis, & ex donis ministerialibus ad aedificationem Ecclesiae datis — quae tamen non tollunt inevidentiam fidei, nec efficiunt ut mysteria fiant evidenter visa.

5. Unde concludimus, nullum dari in viatoribus lumen clarius lumine fidei quoad modum cognoscendi; lumen gloriae solis comprehensoribus in patria competit.
english: Article VII. Whether there is given to wayfarers any light clearer than the light of faith.

1. Theology divides into wayfarers' and comprehensors' — of the way and of the homeland. The first rests on faith's light; the second on glory's. Is any clearer light given to wayfarers so that they know faith's mysteries evidently?

2. Papists and some Scholastics posit a prophetic light or gift of understanding by which Church doctors judge mysteries more clearly than ordinary believers. The Orthodox deny any light clearer than faith as to the thing's evidence — though faith's own light may admit degrees of extension and firmness.

3. Faith's notion involves inevidence. A clearer light that made faith's objects evident would turn them into objects of science or vision. In the way there is not vision of God but faith: we walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7).

4. That learned theologians grasp and explain more credibles comes from greater learning, Scripture study, and ministerial gifts for edification — not from a light above faith. Those gifts do not remove inevidence or make mysteries seen.
5. No light clearer than faith as to the mode of knowing is given to wayfarers. Glory's light belongs only to comprehensors in the homeland.

ART. VIII.
In quo solvuntur tres quaestiones. Prima est, An fides bene distinguatur in infusam, & acquisitam. Secunda est, An fides sit certior ipsis scientiis. Tertia est, Quid sit proprie credere in Deum.

1. Prima quaestio: An fides bene distinguatur in infusam & acquisitam. Scholastici distinguunt fidem in infusam (quam DEUS per gratiam creat in anima) & acquisitam (quam homo studio & doctrina comparat). Orthodoxi fatentur dari fidem historicam seu acquisitam, quae etiam daemonibus & hypocritis inesse potest; sed fidem justificantem & salvificam negant esse acquisitam: ea enim est donum DEI, Spiritu Sancto infusum, non humana industria partum.

2. Secunda quaestio: An fides sit certior ipsis scientiis. Respondemus fidem divinam esse certiorem qualibet scientia creata, non quidem quoad evidentiam (nam scientia est evidens, fides inevidens), sed quoad firmitatem fundamenti: nititur enim DEI testimonio, qui nec fallere nec falli potest; scientiae vero nituntur mediis creatis, quae quamvis sint certa, non adaequant infallibilitatem DEI.

3. Tertia quaestio: Quid sit proprie credere in Deum. Distinguendum est inter credere DEUM, credere DEO, & credere in DEUM. Credere DEUM, est credere DEUM esse. Credere DEO, est credere eis quae DEUS dicit. Credere in DEUM, est fiducialiter in DEUM tanquam in salutis authorem recumbere — quod est proprium fidei justificantis, & non competit daemonibus, qui credunt & contremiscunt.
english: Article VIII. Three questions solved: whether faith is well divided into infused and acquired; whether faith is more certain than the sciences; what it is properly to believe in God.

1. Infused vs acquired. Scholastics distinguish faith God creates by grace in the soul from faith gained by study and teaching. The Orthodox grant historical or acquired faith — even in demons and hypocrites — but deny that justifying, saving faith is acquired. It is God's gift, infused by the Spirit, not born of human industry.

2. Is faith more certain than the sciences? Divine faith is more certain than any created science — not as to evidence (science is evident; faith inevident), but as to the foundation's firmness. Faith rests on God's testimony, who can neither deceive nor be deceived; the sciences rest on created middles that, however certain, do not equal God's infallibility.

3. What is it properly to believe in God? Distinguish: believing that God is; believing God (what he says); and believing in God — resting trustingly on God as salvation's author. That last is proper to justifying faith and does not belong to demons, who believe and tremble.
