ART. IX.
Refellitur Sententia Nicolai Grevinchovii, dicentis habitum fidei non esse infusum, sed acquisitum.

1. Nicolaus Grevinchovius, Remonstrantium Theologus, asserit habitum fidei non infundi a DEO, sed ab homine acquiri per usum mediiorum & assiduam verbi auditionem — perinde ac habitus scientiarum & artium acquiruntur. Hanc sententiam Orthodoxi rejiciunt.

2. Primo, quia Scriptura fidem appellat donum DEI, non opus humanum: Ephes.2.8. gratia estis salvati per fidem; & hoc non ex vobis, DEI donum est. Philipp.1.29. vobis donatum est in CHRISTUM credere.

3. Secundo, quia fides justificans est supernaturalis, & objectum habet mysteria captum naturae superantia; ergo non potest acquiri viribus naturae, sed requirit specialem DEI infusionem & Spiritus Sancti operationem.

4. Tertio, quia si fides esset habitus acquisitus, differret solum gradu a fide historica daemonum & hypocriticorum; at Scriptura & Ecclesiae consensus docent fidem salvificam specie differre, utpote quae charitatem & fiduciam secum fert, & a Spiritu Sancto regenerante producitur.

5. Quarto, Grevinchovii sententia viam sternit Pelagianismo & Arminianismo, tribuendo homini vires credendi ex se, absque speciali gratiae praevenientis & operantis auxilio. Ideoque rejicienda est.
english: Article IX. The opinion of Nicolaas Grevinchoven is refuted — that the habit of faith is not infused but acquired.

1. Grevinchoven, a Remonstrant, holds that faith's habit is not infused by God but acquired by using the means and hearing the word diligently — as arts and sciences are acquired. The Orthodox reject this.
2. Scripture calls faith God's gift, not a human work (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29 — it has been granted to you to believe in Christ).
3. Justifying faith is supernatural; its objects surpass nature's grasp. It cannot be acquired by nature's powers; it needs God's infusion and the Spirit's operation.

4. If faith were merely acquired, it would differ only in degree from demons' and hypocrites' historical faith. Scripture and the Church teach that saving faith differs in kind — bringing charity and trust, produced by the regenerating Spirit.
5. Grevinchoven's view opens onto Pelagianism and Arminianism, giving man power to believe from himself without special prevenient and operating grace. It is to be rejected.

source_text:
ART. X.
An fides actualis aut habitualis infantibus insit, aut inesse possit.

1. Assertio prima: Non est impossibile, absolute loquendo, fidem tum actualem, tum habitualem infantibus inesse. De fide habituali res est manifesta: nam infantes, in statu integritatis, nati fuissent cum habitibus supernaturalibus; & in statu corruptionis, DEUS potest per Spiritum Sanctum habitum fidei in infantium animis creare, sicut in adultis.

2. De fide actuali difficilior est quaestio. Nonnulli negant infantes ullos actus intellectus exercere posse. Alii, cum Augustino & multis Orthodoxis, fatentur DEUM posse in infantibus elicere actus fidei occultos & ineffabiles, modo sibi noto — praesertim in baptismo, ubi Spiritus Sanctus in foederatis infantibus operatur.

3. Assertio secunda: Etsi possibile sit fidem infantibus inesse, non tamen tenemur asserere omnes infantes baptizatos actu fidem habere; salus infantium foederatorum nititur DEI promissione & CHRISTI merito, non demonstrabili praesentia actus fidei in iis.

4. Assertio tertia: Fides parentum, seu fides Ecclesiae, non est formaliter fides infantium; nec Papistarum fictio de fide aliena (fide Ecclesiae infantibus imputata) admittenda est. Infantes foederati salvantur non aliena fide tanquam formali principio in se, sed DEI gratia in CHRISTO, cujus signum & sigillum baptismus est.

5. Quod ad adultos attinet, fides actualis & habitualis utraque requiritur ad justificationem: habitus ut principium, actus ut exercitium quo CHRISTUS apprehenditur.
english: Article X. Whether actual or habitual faith is in infants, or can be in them.

1. First: it is not absolutely impossible for infants to have both actual and habitual faith. Habitual faith is plain enough — in integrity infants would have been born with supernatural habits; in corruption God can create faith's habit in their souls by the Spirit, as in adults.

2. Actual faith is harder. Some deny infants any intellective acts. Others, with Augustine and many Orthodox, grant that God can elicit in them hidden, ineffable acts of faith in a manner known to himself — especially in baptism, where the Spirit works in covenanted infants.

3. Second: possibility does not bind us to assert that every baptized infant actually has faith. Covenanted infants' salvation rests on God's promise and Christ's merit, not on a demonstrable act of faith in them.

4. Third: parents' or the Church's faith is not formally the infants' faith. The Papist fiction of alien faith imputed to infants is rejected. Covenanted infants are saved by God's grace in Christ — baptism its sign and seal — not by alien faith as a formal principle in them.
5. In adults both habitual and actual faith are required for justification: habit as principle, act as the exercise that apprehends Christ.

source_text:
ART. XI.
An in Daemonibus sit fides.

1. Quaeritur an daemones fidem habeant. Scriptura dicit, Jacob.2.19. daemones credunt & contremiscunt. Unde colligitur iis inesse aliquam fidem.

2. Distinguendum tamen est: fides quae daemonibus inest, est fides historica seu dogmatica — assensus intellectus de veritate eorum quae DEUS revelavit — non fides justificans seu fiducialis. Credunt DEUM esse, & multa de CHRISTO vera esse; sed non recumbunt in CHRISTUM ut Salvatorem, nec amant DEUM.

3. Unde Augustinus & Scholastici: fides daemonum est sine dilectione & sine fiducia; ideoque mortua est, & ad salutem non confert. Fides salvifica formatur charitate (ut loquuntur), seu potius a charitate & fiducia inseparabilis est in adultis.

4. Bonaventura & alii quaerunt an fides daemonum sit fidei habitus infusus. Respondemus eam potius esse notitiam acquisitam ex experientia & revelationibus, non habitum gratiae; nam gratia sanctificans daemonibus non inest.
english: Article XI. Whether there is faith in demons.
1. Do demons have faith? James 2:19 — the demons believe and tremble — shows some faith is in them.

2. Distinguish: theirs is historical or dogmatic faith — intellective assent to what God revealed — not justifying or fiducial faith. They believe that God is and that much about Christ is true; they do not rest on Christ as Savior or love God.
3. So Augustine and the Scholastics: demons' faith is without love and trust — dead, and of no avail for salvation. Saving faith in adults is inseparable from charity and trust.
4. Is demons' faith an infused habit? Rather it is knowledge from experience and revelations, not a habit of grace — sanctifying grace is not in them.

source_text:
ART. XII.
An fides fuerit in anima CHRISTI? & an sit in Sanctis, qui jam in coelum translati, habeant DEI cognitionem facialem, ut loquuntur.

1. De fide in anima CHRISTI: Theologi Orthododoxi communiter negant fidem fuisse in anima CHRISTI viatoris eodem modo quo in nobis, quia CHRISTUS a primo conceptionis momento visionem DEI claram & beatificam habuit; fides autem & visio simul in eodem subjecto quoad idem objectum non consistunt.

2. Aliqui tamen distinguunt: CHRISTUS ut viator quaedam per fidem cognovit quoad statum externaе humiliationis; sed tutius est dicere cognitionem ejus de rebus divinis semper fuisse superiorem fide, quia personaliter unitus erat Λόγῳ.

3. De Sanctis in coelo: illi non habent fidem, sed visionem. Fides evacuatur in patria, 1 Cor.13. Cum enim videbimus facie ad faciem, non amplius per fidem ambulamus. Habent cognitionem facialem DEI — non quidem comprehensionem infinitam, sed visionem intuitivam & beatificam secundum capacitam creaturae.
english: Article XII. Whether there was faith in Christ's soul; and whether the saints already translated to heaven have face-to-face knowledge of God.

1. Orthodox theologians commonly deny that faith was in Christ's soul as in ours. From conception he had clear beatific vision of God; faith and vision do not coexist in the same subject about the same object.
2. Some say Christ as wayfarer knew some things by faith in his outward humiliation. Safer: his knowledge of divine things was always above faith, because he was personally united to the Logos.

3. Saints in heaven have not faith but vision. Faith is evacuated in the homeland (1 Corinthians 13). Seeing face to face, they no longer walk by faith. They have facial knowledge of God — not infinite comprehension, but intuitive beatific vision according to creaturely capacity.

source_text:
ART. XIII.
An recte negent Remonstrantes, Adamum ante lapsum habuisse potentiam credendi in Christum.

1. Remonstrantes negant Adamum in statu integritatis habuisse potentiam seu habitum credendi in CHRISTUM mediatorem — quia (inquiunt) promissio de semine mulieris post lapsum demum data est, & objectum fidei justificantis tunc nondum erat revelatum.

2. Orthodoxi respondent: Adamum ante lapsum habuisse potentiam obedientiае & fiduciae in DEUM Creatorem & Dominum; & virtualiter seu in radice habuisse potentiam credendi in Mediatorem, si DEUS eum revelasset — quia intellectus & voluntas ejus recta erant, & ad omne bonum supernaturale a DEO revelandum potens.

3. Quod vero actu non crediderit in CHRISTUM ante lapsum, concedimus: quia mysterium incarnationis & redemptionis nondum erat revelatum. Sed potentia remota non est neganda.

4. Remonstrantium negatio eo tendit, ut fidem justificantem faciant mere historicam & contingentem revelationi post lapsum, & ut gratiae praevenientis necessitatem in lapso minuant. Ideo rejicienda.
english: Article XIII. Whether the Remonstrants rightly deny that Adam before the fall had the power of believing in Christ.

1. Remonstrants deny that Adam in integrity had power or habit to believe in Christ the mediator — the woman's-seed promise came only after the fall, they say, and justifying faith's object was not yet revealed.

2. Orthodox answer: Adam had power of obedience and trust in God as Creator and Lord; and virtually, in the root, power to believe in the Mediator if God had revealed him — his intellect and will were right and able for every supernatural good God might reveal.
3. That he did not actually believe in Christ before the fall we grant — incarnation and redemption were not yet revealed. Remote power is not to be denied.
4. Their denial tends to make justifying faith merely historical and tied to post-fall revelation, and to lessen prevenient grace's necessity in the fallen. Rejected.

source_text:
ART. XIV.
An objectum fidei possit esse falsum.

1. Non desunt qui asserant objectum fidei posse esse falsum — si DEUS (per impossibile) falsum revelaret, vel si aliquis credat id quod de facto falsum est, putans a DEO revelatum.

2. Respondemus: Objectum fidei divinae, formaliter spectatum, non potest esse falsum; quia fides divina nititur DEI testimonio, qui est ipsa veritas & nec fallere nec falli potest. Si quid falsum creditur, non est fides divina, sed error vel fides humana fallax.

3. Quod aliqui dicunt de fide quae versatur circa propositiones conditionales vel de futuris contingentibus, non facit objectum fidei esse falsum: DEUS enim vera revelat, etiam de contingentibus, secundum decretum suum.
english: Article XIV. Whether the object of faith can be false.
1. Some say faith's object can be false — if God (per impossibile) revealed a falsehood, or if someone believes what is in fact false, taking it as revealed.

2. Formally, divine faith's object cannot be false. It rests on God's testimony; he is truth itself and can neither deceive nor be deceived. Believing a falsehood is error or fallacious human faith, not divine faith.
3. Faith about conditionals or future contingents does not make the object false: God reveals what is true, even about contingents, according to his decree.

source_text:
ART. XV.
Quomodo solvendum sit illud argumentum Remonstrantium: Quod unusquisque tenetur credere, illud est verum, &c.

1. Remonstrantes argumentantur: Unusquisque tenetur credere CHRISTUM pro se mortuum esse; At quod unusquisque tenetur credere, est verum; Ergo CHRISTUS pro omnibus & singulis mortuus est — etiam pro reprobis.

2. Orthodoxi tribus modis respondere solent: negando majorem; distinguendo minorem; vel negando minorem. Primus modus (negare majorem) non satis tutus videtur; ne sequatur DEUM praecipere reprobis credenda quae falsa sunt.

3. Tutior responsio: praeceptum credendi CHRISTUM pro se mortuum esse non obligat absolute omnes & singulos absque conditione, sed sub conditione conversionis & resipiscentiae — h.e. eos qui agnoscunt peccata & dolorem de iis concipiunt, vox Evangelii jubet ut credant CHRISTUM pro ipsis mortuum esse.

4. Reprobi non tenentur credere se esse electos, nec CHRISTUM pro ipsis quatenus in malitia permanentibus mortuum esse; tenentur converti & credere secundum Evangelii doctrinam. Infidelitas qua damnantur non est mera negatio assensus historici, sed refractaria impoenitentia.

5. Ita tollitur sophisma Remonstrantium, & doctrina satisfactionis particularis (pro electis) cum universali Evangelii proclamatione conciliatur.
english: Article XV. How that Remonstrant argument is to be solved: that whatever each is bound to believe is true.
1. Remonstrants argue: each is bound to believe Christ died for him; whatever one is bound to believe is true; therefore Christ died for all and each — even the reprobate.
2. Orthodox answers: deny the major, distinguish the minor, or deny the minor. Denying the major is unsafe — as if God commanded the reprobate to believe falsehoods.

3. Safer: the precept to believe Christ died for you does not bind absolutely without condition, but under conversion and repentance. Those who own their sins and sorrow for them are commanded to believe Christ died for them.

4. The reprobate are not bound to believe they are elect, or that Christ died for them as they remain in malice; they are bound to convert and believe the Gospel. The unbelief that damns is refractory impenitence, not mere denial of historical assent.
5. So the sophism falls, and particular satisfaction for the elect stands with the Gospel's universal proclamation.

source_text:
ART. XVI.
An fides sit assensus discursivus? Et an Pontificii utantur circulari discursu in stabilienda fide.

1. Assensus dividi solet in simplicem (noeticum) & dianoeticum seu discursivum. Simplex assensus est, quo intellectus assentitur propositionibus sua luce claris & manifestis. Discursivus, quo assentitur conclusioni propter praemissas.

2. Fides divina est assensus discursivus: assentimur articulis fidei propter hoc medium — DEUS dixit, seu Scriptura testatur. Non est assensus simplex noeticus, quia mysteria fidei non sunt per se nota lumine naturae.

3. Pontificii in stabilienda fide utuntur discursu circulari: Scripturam esse DEI verbum probant ex Ecclesiae testimonio; Ecclesiam esse infallibilem probant ex Scriptura. Hic circulus vitiosus est, & fidem divinam destruere tendit.

4. Orthodoxi negant circulum: principium fidei est ipsum DEI verbum seipsum authenticans per notas intrinsecas & testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum — non Ecclesiae Romanае authoritas tanquam fundamentum primum.
english: Article XVI. Whether faith is a discursive assent; and whether the Papists use a circular discourse in establishing faith.
1. Assent is simple (noetic) — to propositions clear by their own light — or discursive (dianoetic) — to a conclusion because of premises.
2. Divine faith is discursive: we assent to the articles because God has spoken, or Scripture testifies. It is not simple noetic assent; faith's mysteries are not self-evident to nature's light.
3. Papists establish faith by a vicious circle: Scripture is God's word because the Church says so; the Church is infallible because Scripture says so. That tends to destroy divine faith.
4. Orthodox deny the circle. Faith's principle is God's word authenticating itself by intrinsic marks and the Spirit's internal testimony — not Rome's authority as first foundation.

source_text:
ART. XVII.
An notitia sit actus ab habitu fidei elicitus.

1. Robertus Bellarminus lib.1. de justificatione cap.7. dicit, fidem non esse notitiam, sed assensum; & notitiam esse praerequisitam ad fidem, non ipsum fidei actum.

2. Distinguendum est inter notitias: (1) notitia terminorum; (2) notitia propositionis ut proponitur; (3) notitia seu judicium quo assentimur. Primae duae praerequiruntur ad assensum fidei; tertia est vel ipse assensus, vel ei intimius conjuncta.

3. Fides justificans non est nuda notitia historica, sed assensus fiducialis; ideoque Bellarmini distinctio, si eo tendat ut fidem a notitia prorsus sejungat, rejicienda est. Orthodoxi docent in fide inesse notitiam & assensum, imo & fiduciam.
english: Article XVII. Whether knowledge is an act elicited from the habit of faith.
1. Bellarmine says faith is assent, not knowledge — knowledge only a prerequisite, not faith's own act.
2. Distinguish: knowledge of terms; of the proposition as proposed; and the judgment by which we assent. The first two precede faith's assent; the third is assent itself or joined to it.
3. Justifying faith is not bare historical knowledge but fiducial assent. If Bellarmine severs faith from knowledge entirely, reject that. Orthodox: faith includes knowledge, assent, and trust.

source_text:
ART. XVIII.
An fiducia sit actus fidei.

1. Theologi Orthodoxi non eodem modo loquuntur de fiducia. Alii fiduciam esse ipsum fidei actum justificantem; alii eam esse actum a fide distinctum, etsi inseparabilem; alii fiduciam pluribus modis accipi.

2. Fiducia accipi potest: (1) ut firma persuasio de DEI misericordia in CHRISTO; (2) ut recumbentia in DEI promissis; (3) ut animosa oppositio contra pericula & miserias; (4) ut gaudium & pax conscientiae de remissione jam impetrata.

3. Nos cum plerisque Orthodoxis: fiducia justificans est actus fidei — seu potius fides justificans essentialiter includit fiduciam, qua CHRISTUS & promissiones gratiae nobis applicantur. Non est mere notitia historica, nec nuda assensio dogmatica.

4. Bellarmini sententia, fiduciam certitudinis de remissione particulari non posse haberi in hac vita absque revelatione speciali, rejicitur: Scriptura fideles hortatur ad fiduciam, & signa regeneratis dat quibus de sua in CHRISTO participatione certi reddantur.
english: Article XVIII. Whether trust is an act of faith.
1. Orthodox theologians differ on trust: some identify it with faith's justifying act; some call it distinct but inseparable; some take trust in several senses.
2. Trust may mean: firm persuasion of God's mercy in Christ; resting on his promises; courageous stance against dangers and miseries; or joy and peace of conscience over remission already obtained.

3. With most Orthodox: justifying trust is an act of faith — or justifying faith essentially includes the trust by which Christ and grace's promises are applied to us. Not mere historical knowledge or bare dogmatic assent.
4. Bellarmine's claim that certainty of particular remission needs special revelation in this life is rejected. Scripture urges trust and gives the regenerate signs of their share in Christ.

source_text:
ART. XIX.
An fiducia sit actus intellectus, & quomodo differat ab assensu.

1. Quaeritur an fiducia sit in intellectu an in voluntate. Pontificii plerumque fiduciam ad voluntatem referunt. Orthodoxi distinguunt.

2. Fiducia, quatenus est firma persuasio & judicium mentis de DEI promissione, est actus intellectus, & non differt realiter ab assensu fidei, sed ratione: assensus respicit veritatem testimonii; fiducia respicit bonitatem rei promissae ut mihi applicabilis.

3. Fiducia, quatenus est amorosus in DEUM motus & recumbentia voluntatis, est actus voluntatis, a fide inseparabilis in justificato, sed formaliter distinctus.

4. Sententia Orthodоxa mediа: tota fides justificans est in intellectu tanquam in subjecto proprio quoad assensum & persuasionem; sed ad voluntatem pertinet ratione originis (a voluntate imperata), ratione concomitantiae (charitas), & ratione fructuum.
english: Article XIX. Whether trust is an act of the intellect, and how it differs from assent.
1. Is trust in the intellect or the will? Papists commonly put it in the will. Orthodox distinguish.

2. As firm persuasion about God's promise, trust is an intellective act — not really distinct from faith's assent, but in reason: assent regards the testimony's truth; trust regards the promised good as applicable to me.
3. As loving motion and the will's resting on God, trust is a will-act — inseparable from faith in the justified, formally distinct.
4. Middle Orthodox view: justifying faith as assent and persuasion is in the intellect as proper subject; it belongs to the will by origin (will-commanded), concomitance (charity), and fruits.

source_text:
ART. XX.
Utrum objectum fidei salvificae sit remissio peccatorum jam impetrata? An vero sit remissio peccatorum impetranda & obtinenda: Ubi obiter solvitur praecipuum argumentum Bellarmini, contra objectum & naturam fidei justificantis.

1. Quaeritur an objectum fidei justificantis sit remissio jam habita, an potius CHRISTUS & promissio remissionis obtinendae per fidem.

2. Nos cum Orthodoxis: objectum fidei justificantis primarium est CHRISTUS Mediator, & DEI promissio in ipso; fides justificat non quia credit remissionem jam formaliter inesse, sed quia CHRISTUM apprehendit, in quo remissio offertur & per fidem applicatur.

3. Bellarmini argumentum — si fides esset fiducia remissionis particularis jam habitae, praesupponeret justificationem quam dicitur causare — solvitur: fides non praesupponit remissionem tanquam jam inhaerentem ante fidem, sed eam consequitur & applicat; objectum est promissio & CHRISTUS, non remissio tanquam praevia possessio.
english: Article XX. Whether the object of saving faith is remission of sins already obtained, or remission to be obtained.
1. Is justifying faith's object remission already had, or Christ and the promise of remission through faith?

2. With the Orthodox: the primary object is Christ the Mediator and God's promise in him. Faith justifies not by believing remission already formally inheres, but by apprehending Christ, in whom remission is offered and by faith applied.

3. Bellarmine: if faith were trust of particular remission already had, it would presuppose the justification it causes. Solved: faith does not presuppose remission as inhering before faith; it follows and applies it. The object is the promise and Christ — not remission as prior possession.

source_text:
ART. XXI.
An & quatenus fides ad voluntatem pertineat.

1. Guilielmus Estius dicit fidem ad voluntatem pertinere. Alii fidem totam in intellectu collocant. Nos distinguimus.

2. Fides quoad assensum & judicium est in intellectu tanquam in subjecto proprio. Ad voluntatem tamen pertinet: (1) ratione originis — quia voluntas imperat intellectui ut attendat & assentiatur; (2) ratione status — quia fides dirigit voluntatem; (3) ratione fructuum — quia ex fide nascuntur in voluntate amor, fiducia, obedientia.

3. Haec sententia differt ab Estii, quia non refert fidem ad voluntatem ratione suae originis solius tanquam in voluntate subjectatae, sed ratione imperii, concomitantiае, & fructuum.
english: Article XXI. Whether and how far faith belongs to the will.
1. Estius puts faith with the will; others put it wholly in the intellect. We distinguish.

2. As assent and judgment, faith is in the intellect as proper subject. It still belongs to the will: by origin (the will commands the intellect to attend and assent); by state (faith directs the will); by fruits (love, trust, obedience born from faith in the will).
3. Unlike Estius, we do not seat faith in the will by origin alone, but relate it to the will by command, concomitance, and fruits.

source_text:
ART. XXII.
Utrum Charitas sit forma fidei.

1. Pontificii, sequentes Scholasticos quosdam, docent charitatem esse formam fidei — ita ut fides sine charitate sit informis & mortua, & per charitatem formetur ad justificandum.

2. Orthodoxi rejiciunt: fides justificans non formatur a charitate tanquam a forma accidentali extrinseca; sed ipsa fides, quatenus est viva & fiducialis, justificat ante charitatem formaliter consideratam — quamvis charitas fidei vivae inseparabiliter concomitatur.

3. Fides mortua (historica sine fiducia) non est eadem specie cum fide justificante; non indiget charitate ut formetur, sed regenerante Spiritus operatione ut fiat viva.
english: Article XXII. Whether charity is the form of faith.
1. Papists, after some Scholastics, make charity faith's form — faith without charity unformed and dead, formed by charity unto justification.

2. Orthodox reject this. Justifying faith is not shaped by charity as an extrinsic accidental form. Living fiducial faith justifies before charity formally considered — though charity inseparably accompanies living faith.
3. Dead (merely historical) faith is not the same kind as justifying faith. It needs not charity to "form" it, but the regenerating Spirit to make it living.

source_text:
ART. XXIII.
An Religio sit virtus Theologica a Fide distincta.

1. Thomas Aquinas 2.2. q.81 docet religionem esse virtutem moralem (non theologicam), qua DEO cultus debitus redditur. Alii eam virtutem theologicam a fide distinctam faciunt.

2. Nos: Religio late sumpta includit totum DEI cultum, & sic non est virtus a fide, spe, charitate realiter distincta, sed earum exercitium erga DEUM. Stricte, ut virtus specialis dirigendi cultus actus, potest a fide distingui, non tamen est virtus theologica eodem modo quo fides, spes, charitas — quia objectum ejus formale non est DEUS ut finis supernaturalis per revelationem, sed cultus debitus.
english: Article XXIII. Whether religion is a theological virtue distinct from faith.
1. Aquinas makes religion a moral virtue (not theological) rendering due worship to God. Others call it a theological virtue distinct from faith.

2. Broadly, religion is whole worship of God — not really distinct from faith, hope, and charity, but their exercise toward God. Strictly, as directing worship, it can be told apart from faith, yet is not theological in the same sense as faith, hope, and charity: its formal object is due worship, not God as supernatural end by revelation.

source_text:
ART. XXIV.
Ostenditur Theologiam Viatorum tribus modis accipi: & probatur Theologiam primo modo acceptam, non esse habitum a Fide re distinctum.

1. Theologia viatorum tribus modis accipitur: (1) pro ipsa fide divina, qua mysteria revelata credimus; (2) pro habitu scientifico quo ex principiis fidei conclusiones theologicae deducuntur — ut quidam Scholastici volunt; (3) pro habitu aggregato ex fide & disciplinis philosophicis, quo Scholastica Theologia constat.

2. Theologia primo modo accepta non est habitus a fide realiter distinctus: est ipsa fides, seu notitia fidei. Qui aliter distinguunt, multiplicant habitus sine necessitate.
english: Article XXIV. That the theology of wayfarers is taken in three ways; and that theology in the first sense is not a habit really distinct from faith.

1. Wayfarers' theology three ways: (1) divine faith itself believing revealed mysteries; (2) a "scientific" habit deducing theological conclusions from faith's principles (some Scholastics); (3) an aggregate from faith and philosophy — scholastic theology.
2. In the first sense theology is not really distinct from faith — it is faith itself. Other distinctions multiply habits without need.

source_text:
ART. XXV.
Probatur, contra Antonium Ruvium, Theologiam secundo modo acceptam, non esse scientiam, sed fidem divinam.

1. Antonius Ruvius asserit Theologiam (ut conclusiones ex principiis fidei deducit) esse veram scientiam. Nos negamus.

2. Scientia propria Aristotelis nititur principiis per se notis & evidenter visis. At principia Theologiae (articuli fidei) non sunt evidenter visa, sed credita. Ergo discursus theologicus ex illis non gignit scientiam proprie dictam, sed fidem discursivam seu conclusionem fidelem.

3. Dici potest Theologia esse scientia lato modo, seu sapientia; sed non scientia Aristotelica stricte.
english: Article XXV. Against Antonio Rubio: that theology in the second sense is not science but divine faith.
1. Rubio calls theology (deducing from faith's principles) true science. We deny it.

2. Aristotelian science rests on self-evident, evidently seen principles. Theology's principles (articles of faith) are believed, not seen. Discourse from them yields discursive faith — a faithful conclusion — not science properly so called.
3. Theology may be called science broadly, or wisdom — not Aristotelian science strictly.

source_text:
ART. XXVI.
Probatur Theologiam tertio modo acceptam, hoc est, Theologiam Scholasticam esse habitum aggregatum ex Fide, & Philosophicis disciplinis.

1. Theologia Scholastica utitur principiis fidei & simul mediis philosophicis (logica, metaphysica, ethica) ad conclusiones explicandas & defendendas.

2. Ideo non est habitus simplex, sed aggregatum ex fide & habitibus philosophicis. Beneficio Logicae disponit argumenta; Metaphysicae explicat terminos entis & causarum; Ethicae virtutes & vitia decalogi.
english: Article XXVI. That theology in the third sense — scholastic theology — is an aggregate habit from faith and the philosophical disciplines.
1. Scholastic theology uses faith's principles together with philosophical middles — logic, metaphysics, ethics — to explain and defend conclusions.
2. So it is not a simple habit but an aggregate of faith and philosophical habits: logic for arguments, metaphysics for being and causes, ethics for the Decalogue's virtues and vices.

source_text:
ART. XXVII.
Theologiam esse similem omnibus habitibus Aristotelicis; praecipue vero prudentiae.

1. Theologia (lato modo) assimilatur habitibus intellectualibus Aristotelis: intelligentiae, scientiae, sapientiae, arti, prudentiae — non quod sit eadem cum illis, sed quod analogice eorum munera in suo ordine impleat.

2. Praecipue assimilatur prudentiae: quia sicut prudentia dirigit actiones humanas ad finem, ita Theologia dirigit intellectum & vitam ad finem supernaturalem — DEI gloriam & salutem aeternam — secundum normas a DEO revelatas.
english: Article XXVII. That theology resembles every Aristotelian intellectual habit — and prudence most of all.

1. Taken broadly, theology is compared to Aristotle's five intellectual habits (understanding, science, wisdom, art, prudence). The point is analogy of office in theology's own order, not identity with those habits.

2. The closest likeness is prudence. Prudence steers human action toward an end; theology steers mind and life toward the supernatural end — God's glory and eternal salvation — by the norms God has revealed.

source_text:
ART. XXVIII.
Utrum Theologia sit disciplina speculativa, an practica.

1. In hac controversia variae sunt Philosophorum & Theologorum sententiae. Alii Theologiam mere speculativam; alii mere practicam; alii mixtam faciunt.

2. Nos: Theologia viatorum est principaliter practica, quia finis ejus ultimus non est nuda contemplatio, sed fruitio DEI per fidem, spem, charitatem, & obedientiam — etsi multa in ea speculativa continentur.

3. Theologia patriae est magis speculativa seu contemplativa, quia in visione DEI terminatur. Attamen etiam in via Theologia non excludit speculationem; sed ordinat eam ad praxim pietatis.
english: Article XXVIII. Whether theology is a speculative or a practical discipline.
1. Opinions vary: merely speculative, merely practical, or mixed.

2. Wayfarers' theology is principally practical — its ultimate end is not bare contemplation but enjoyment of God through faith, hope, charity, and obedience — though it contains much that is speculative.
3. Homeland theology is more speculative or contemplative, ending in God's vision. Even in the way, theology does not shut out speculation; it orders it to the practice of piety.

source_text:
ART. XXIX.
An Theologia Viatorum dici possit speculativa a speculatione, seu visione, qua futura est in patria.

1. Quidam Theologiam viae speculativam dicunt a fine — visione DEI in patria. Sed hoc confundit Theologiam viae cum Theologia patriae.

2. Respondemus: Theologia viatorum non est speculativa a visione futura tanquam a forma sua praesenti; nam forma praesens est fides, non visio. Dici potest ordinari ad speculationem patriae ut ad finem; sed non inde mere speculativa in via.
english: Article XXIX. Whether the theology of wayfarers can be called speculative from the speculation or vision that will be in the homeland.
1. Some call way-theology speculative from its end — God's vision in the homeland. That confuses way-theology with homeland theology.

2. Wayfarers' theology is not speculative from future vision as its present form — the present form is faith, not vision. It is ordered to homeland speculation as end; it is not merely speculative in the way.

source_text:
ART. XXX.
An vera & proprie dicta Theologia possit esse in homine impio, seu non regenerato.

1. Quaeritur an homo impius — hypocrita, haereticus, aut mere literatus — veram Theologiam habere possit.

2. Si Theologia sumatur pro nuda notitia historica articulorum & conclusionum Scholasticarum, potest inesse impio: daemones & hypocritaе multa vera de DEO sciunt.

3. Si Theologia sumatur proprie pro sapientia salvifica, seu fide viva conjuncta cum timore DEI & obedientia, non potest inesse impio non regenerato: quia talis Theologia est donum Spiritus Sancti, a charitate & fide salvifica inseparabilis.

4. Ideo concludimus: Theologiam proprie dictam non esse in impiis; quamvis notitiam theologicam acquisitam & historiam fidei in iis dari concedamus. FINIS Exercitationis Tertiae.
english: Article XXX. Whether true and properly so-called theology can be in an ungodly human being.
1. Can an ungodly person — hypocrite, heretic, or merely learned — have true theology?
2. As bare historical knowledge of articles and scholastic conclusions: yes. Demons and hypocrites know many true things about God.
3. As saving wisdom — living faith with fear of God and obedience: no. That theology is the Spirit's gift, inseparable from charity and saving faith.
4. Conclusion: theology properly so called is not in the ungodly; acquired theological knowledge and faith's history may be. End of the Third Exercise.
